narrative: The model estimated a 45% chance that you will leave. That is a borderline signal—slightly below an even chance—but it was treated as a leave risk when the promotion decision was made. The strongest factor was your overall years of experience. With one to five years, you match the most common group among employees predicted to stay (about half), so this pushed toward staying. The second factor was other job opportunities. You reported none, and most employees predicted to stay also had none (about 77%), so this also reduced the leaving signal. The third factor was ease of getting involved in your job. You found it difficult to participate in decisions and share opinions, which pushed toward leaving; only about one in ten employees predicted to stay found involvement difficult. Although the first two drivers leaned toward staying, difficult engagement contributed to the 45% estimate. Because the risk is borderline and partly driven by an involvement barrier, the organization should not treat promotion denial as final. Consider reviewing decision-making access, role clarity, and support, and reassess your leave risk with updated evidence before making a long-term promotion decision.
